propositions: The byte-equivalence hardening test invokes Pandoc twice per corpus unit (884 total) — once in production _convert and once in a copied _legacy_convert — doubling subprocess overhead; the copied oracle reads live mutable _PANDOC_TO constant instead of pinned historical bytes, making it coupled to production rather than independent.

Mutating production _PANDOC_TO from html to plain changes both production and copied legacy digests identically, proving the copied oracle shares conversion constants with production and does not function as a standalone verification.

Golden fixture schema stores a single platform-specific binary fingerprint (macOS arm64) but CI runs on both macOS arm64 and Ubuntu x86_64, causing cross-platform rejection when the installed Pandoc binary hash differs from the single stored hash.

Replacing the copied _legacy_convert subprocess with immutable golden fixture lookup preserves all 884 real production Pandoc invocations while eliminating 884 redundant copied Pandoc subprocesses and reducing total hardening runtime by ~49 percent.

The fixture regeneration script must deterministically record Pandoc version and platform-aware binary fingerprint map to enable version-drift detection and cross-platform CI validation without weakening the oracle contract.
Production format mutations must fail against the independent immutable expected output, restoring the stated contract that the test proves byte identity to the landed renderer.
